(2020) Liquefaction processes for LH , LNG, and LE are complex with the most notable difference 2 between the liquefaction processes occurring because of the different temperatures that are needed for each fuel to reach a liquid state (see Table 8). For example, hydrogen liquefaction typically requires the use of liquid nitrogen for precooling (−196°C) to bridge most of the temperature gap. However, natural gas and ethane liquefaction can use liquid propane (−40°C) for precooling steps to bridge a considerable temperature gap. Hydrogen liquefaction also requires a catalytic conversion step of ortho-hydrogen (hydrogen with protons that spin in same direction) to para-hydrogen (hydrogen with protons that spin in opposite directions) and uses a helium refrigerant which are not required for LNG or LE production. Because of these process differences, the spatial footprint for liquefaction for each of these fuels will inherently be different as well. More detail on spatial footprint for each of these cryogenic fuels at a selected capacity is shown in Table 8. The Hydrogen Delivery Scenario Analysis Model (HDSAM) estimates hydrogen liquefaction spatial footprint scales according to 0.6 scaling factor which could theoretically be used to put the spatial footprint of liquefaction for each cryogenic fuel on equivalent terms (i.e., area taken up per unit of energy in liquefied fuel per day).
